Coded by DNA in genome. Synthesized on Rough ER.  Synthesis steps: Pre-prohormones to prohormones to hormones. Travel through secretory system: RER to Golgi to membrane through vesicles.
Polar, secreted into bloodstream, and bind on cell surface receptor (polar cannot pass through membrane), initiating transduction pathway by secondary messenger
Not coded in genes; made from enzymes modifying amino acids. Synthesized in specific tissue structures (colloid, thyroid, or chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla).
Amine Hormones (Tyrosine-Derived Hormones) that are polar (move as polar hormones), meaning they are secreted through the transduction pathway and bind at cell surface receptors.

Not coded in genes, derived from enzymes reacting with cholesterol. Synthesized on the smooth ER or in the mitochondria. Bind to cytoplasmic or nuclear receptor after diffusing through the membrane (non-polar). Need carrier proteins to move in blood, and change gene expression in the nucleus
Non-polar Amine (Tyrosine-Derived) Hormones. Need carrier proteins to move in blood. Bind cytoplasmic or nuclear receptor after diffusing through the membrane
Non-polar hormones diffuse into the cell membrane and change gene expression in the nucleus

made from amino acids and sugars (added in Golgi)
Peptide Hormone precursor synthesized directly from mRNA; contains signal peptide and at least one prohormone
Preprohormones are cleaved into prohormones, which is an inert precursor to a hormone. Preprohormones move into Golgi Apparatus for modification into peptide hormones.
packaged into secretory vesicles for release by exocytosis and remain water-soluble in blood. Bind to cell membrane receptors, initiating secondary message cascades

cards.front: Peptide and Steroid Hormone Activation and Lifetimes
cards.back: Peptide hormones are fast acting, but short lived (change from minute to minute). Steroid hormones are slow acting, but long living (take effect on the order of hours, days, months)

Moved by transport proteins in blood stream (non-polar). When arriving at a cell, they diffuse through the membrane and bind to a receptor in the cytosol. The complex moves into the nucleus and activates or represses gene expression.

Proteins have 7 transmembrane domains, and are coupled with a trimeric G protein. G proteins have an alpha, beta, and gamma subunit.

Trimeric (3 subunits (polypeptide chains)); G proteins have 3 subunits: alpha, beta, and gamma. The alpha subunit binds GDP (which can be phosphorylated upon receiving a signal) into in the cell. G_a subunit can dissociate from the rest of the G protein subunits to bind to an effector. G_a subunits can be excitatory (G_as or inhibitory G_ai)

cards.front: Signal Transduction Pathways and Secondary Messengers
cards.back:
A signal molecule (e.g. hormone) can trigger an internal cell signaling pathway controlled by secondary messengers.
Ex)
1. A signal molecule (e.g. peptide, polar hormone) binds to G protein-coupled receptor.
2. G protein turns on Adenylyl Cyclase
3. Adenylyl Cyclase converts ATP into cyclic AMP (cAMP)
4. cAMP activates protein kinase A 
5. protein kinase A phosphorylates other proteins, prompting cascading responses
master gland of endocrine system; located directly above the pituitary gland in the brain; connected to the anterior pituitary by the hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal system.
A hormone that has an endocrine gland as its target
A hormone that targets an organ, organ-system, or tissue (not an endocrine gland)
a capillary bed that drains into another capillary bed through a vein, without going through the heart.
tiny network of blood vessels that carry blood
A special group of nerve cells (with long axons) that connect the hypothalamus to the posterior pituitary gland.
hormones from the hypothalamus travel to the anterior pituitary gland via the bloodstream (portal system) and to the posterior pituitary gland via nerve axons

Direct peptide hormone of the Hypothalamus (secreted into the posterior pituitary gland via neurosecretory cells). Stored in posterior pituitary gland; it is an Anti-Diuretic Hormone -- upon release, causes increased water reabsorption by kidney (urine concentration increases)
Decreases water reabsorption (more water exits body); Inhibits ADH hormones (e.g. Vasopressin)

Direct peptide hormone of the hypothalamus (secreted by neurosecretory cells to be stored in the posterior pituitary gland) and it is secreted during childbirth (positive feedback loop) to increase uterine contractions, and it stimulates milk secretion during infant suckling (positive feedback loop)
Tropic hormone of the Hypothalamus; stimulates GH release by anterior pituitary
Tropic hormone of the Hypothalamus; inhibits GH release and inhibits Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) release by anterior pituitary gland.
Tropic hormone of the Hypothalamus; stimulates anterior pituitary gland to release Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH)
Tropic hormone of the Hypothalamus; stimulates release of Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) and Prolactin by anterior pituitary gland
Tropic hormone of the Hypothalamus; stimulated for release by estrogen; stimulates the anterior pituitary gland to release FSH and LH
Tropic hormone of the Hypothalamus; inhibits prolactin release by anterior pituitary gland
FLAT PEG: FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH, PRL, Endorphins, GH

Direct peptide hormone released by the anterior pituitary gland; stimulates all cells for growth at night -- increases mitosis, cell size, protein synth, metabolism, and fatty acid breakdown | decreases use of glucose for certain cell types
Tropic peptide hormone that stimulates the adrenal cortex to synthesize and secrete glucocorticoids or cortical hormones (during stress)
Tropic peptide hormone that stimulates the thyroid gland to increase in size, absorb iodine, and synth/release Thyroid Hormones (T3 and T4)

Inhibited for release by estrogen and progesterone (from corpus luteum); A tropic peptide hormone, it stimulates ovulation and corpus luteum formation in females and stimulates testosterone synthesis by interstitial cells (in testes) in males
Tropic peptide hormone; in females causes maturation of ovarian follicles. Stimulates maturation of seminiferous tubules in males (for sperm production) -- note direct hormone in males
Direct peptide hormone, promotes lactation in breasts
Direct peptide hormones, inhibit pain perception
Located on top of the kidneys, separated into two parts, the adrenal cortex and the adrenal medulla; the latter wraps around the former.
Outer part of the adrenal glands, responds to ACTH (Adrenocorticotropic Hormone) and synthesizes/secretes corticosteroids
Brain and Spinal Cord
Contains sensory neurons (afferent neurons) and motor neurons (efferent)
Sensor neurons; transmit signals from the environment INTO the nervous system (often CNS)
Motor Neurons; transmit signals from CNS to the rest of the body (e.g. to muscles, glands, or organs)
Gastrointestinal nervous system (controls GI tract)
